title: Polynomial-time computation of planar treewidth
formal:
Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that computes the exact treewidth of every finite planar graph?

Precisely, do there exist one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(M\) and integers \(C,k\ge1\) such that \(M\) halts on every binary input \(x\) within \(C(|x|+1)^k\) transitions and, for every finite simple planar graph \(G\) in the encoding below,
\[
M(\operatorname{enc}(G))=\operatorname{bin}_{\pm}(\operatorname{tw}(G))?
\]
The output is the exact integer treewidth in the specified signed binary encoding. Graph size and treewidth are unrestricted; the polynomial is fixed independently of both. No planar embedding, tree decomposition or bound on treewidth is supplied with the graph.

This is the polynomial-time existence question stated in §4.6 of the 2016 seminar report. It asks for an exact algorithm, not an optimal numerical running-time exponent. A negative answer is the full negation of that existence assertion, not merely an NP-hardness theorem conditional on a separate complexity-class separation.
why: Treewidth is a central measure connecting graph structure with algorithms for otherwise difficult graph problems. An exact polynomial-time algorithm on planar graphs would make optimal width accessible on a large and important sparse graph class. A negative answer would locate a fundamental limitation of planarity despite efficient algorithms for the related branchwidth parameter. The issue is distinct from using a decomposition once one has already been supplied.
status_note: The literal polynomial-time existence question appears in the inspected2016 seminar report and remains explicitly open in the inspected2025 IPEC paper. Cubic-graph hardness and polynomial-delay clique generation have different scopes. A bounded primary review through16September2026, including the new planar excluded-grid preprint, found no matching resolution. Formulation, definitions and theorem scopes were checked; cited full proofs were not independently verified or formalized in Lean.

progress.text: The seminar report poses exact polynomial-time treewidth computation for planar graphs as its Treewidth open problem.
The cubic-graph NP-completeness paper retains the planar case as a separate open question in its conclusion.

The IPEC paper obtains polynomial-delay generation of potential maximal cliques in triconnected planar graphs and an output-sensitive exact treewidth algorithm, while explicitly retaining the general polynomial-time question.
A preprint improves the planar excluded-grid treewidth bound; its stated target is structural rather than the exact computation question.

sentences: Treewidth is the minimum largest-bag size minus one among all tree decompositions of a finite graph.
The question asks whether one deterministic polynomial-time algorithm can compute that integer exactly for every planar graph.
The input is only the finite graph, without a planar embedding, a tree decomposition or a bound on its width.
Inspected results on cubic-graph hardness, polynomial-delay enumeration and planar grid bounds do not establish that polynomial-time algorithm or its nonexistence.
A complete Lean answer must prove the stated uniform algorithm and its bound or prove the full negation for all candidate machines and polynomial bounds.

context_blocks.text: The 2016 seminar report explicitly asks whether the treewidth of a planar graph can be computed in polynomial time. It does not prescribe a fixed exponent, an approximation ratio, a bounded-width promise or a space restriction.

The 2025 potential-maximal-clique paper defines the standard tree decomposition and still describes exact planar treewidth as a long-standing question. Its graph convention is simple, undirected and unweighted; the present card spells out the finite encoding and computational model.

The related branchwidth parameter is polynomial-time computable for planar graphs. The cited sources emphasize that this does not by itself determine exact treewidth, though it supports approximation results.

The 2023 hardness result covers cubic graphs and certain three-dimensional grid subgraphs. Those input classes are not restricted to planar graphs, and its conclusion explicitly retains the planar question as open.

The 2025 algorithm has time polynomial in the graph size multiplied by the number of potential maximal cliques. Its polynomial delay guarantee controls the time between consecutive generated objects, and does not assert that every planar graph has only polynomially many such objects.

A September 2026 preprint improves a structural bound: a planar graph excluding a \(t\times t\) grid minor has treewidth at most \(4t+4\). This is a width-versus-grid theorem, not an exact polynomial-time computation theorem.

source_consolidations.note: The potential-maximal-clique source also raises the complexity of exact treewidth on planar graphs, supplying another occurrence of the retained planar question.
The cubic-graph hardness source supplies context for the still separate planar treewidth problem. Hardness on cubic graphs alone does not establish hardness on planar graphs.

definitions:
A finite simple undirected graph is \(G=(V,E)\), with \(V=[n]=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) for an integer \(n\ge0\), and \(E\) a set of two-element subsets of \(V\). Loops and parallel edges are absent; isolated vertices, disconnected graphs and the empty graph are allowed. Graphs are unweighted. A path is a sequence of distinct vertices with consecutive vertices joined by edges. A cycle is a closed sequence of at least three edges visiting no vertex twice except its starting and ending vertex. A nonempty finite tree is a finite simple connected graph with no cycle; it has a unique path between each pair of its vertices.

A graph is planar if its vertices can be mapped injectively to points of \(\mathbb R^2\), and each edge can be represented by a continuous injective curve \([0,1]\to\mathbb R^2\) whose endpoints are the points of its two vertices, such that no interior point of a curve is a vertex point and distinct edge curves intersect only at common endpoint vertices. The existence of such a drawing is a promise on the input graph; its curves and coordinates are not part of the input. The algorithm is not required to output a drawing.

A tree decomposition is a nonempty finite tree \(T\) with a bag \(B_t\subseteq V\) at each node \(t\in V(T)\), satisfying
\[
\bigcup_{t\in V(T)} B_t=V,
\qquad
\forall\{u,v\}\in E\ \exists t\in V(T):\{u,v\}\subseteq B_t,
\]
and the connectedness condition: for every \(v\in V\), the set \(\{t\in V(T):v\in B_t\}\) induces a connected subtree of \(T\). Equivalently, every node on the unique path between two bags containing \(v\) also has \(v\) in its bag. Empty bags are allowed. The width of this decomposition is \(\max_{t\in V(T)}|B_t|-1\), and
\[
\operatorname{tw}(G)=
\min_{(T,(B_t))\text{ a tree decomposition of }G}
\left(\max_{t\in V(T)}|B_t|-1\right).
\]
The one-node tree with bag \(V\) is a decomposition, so the minimum exists. For the empty graph this convention gives \(-1\); for any nonempty graph it is an integer between \(0\) and \(n-1\). The convention on the single empty graph does not affect polynomial-time solvability.

Encode \(G\) as the bitstring \(1^n0\) followed by exactly \(n(n-1)/2\) bits. These final bits list the indicators of \(\{i,j\}\in E\) in lexicographic order of pairs \((i,j)\) with \(0\le i<j<n\). Thus the encoding length is
\[
L(G)=n+1+\frac{n(n-1)}2.
\]
The empty graph is encoded by the single bit 0. The unary prefix includes every vertex, even if isolated. This explicit adjacency encoding and the ordinary explicit adjacency-list encoding are polynomially interconvertible, so the chosen representation does not alter the polynomial-time question.

The output encoding \(\operatorname{bin}_{\pm}(z)\) for an integer \(z\) is one sign bit, 0 for a nonnegative integer and 1 for a negative integer, followed by the usual base-two representation of \(|z|\), with no leading zero except that zero has magnitude string 0. Negative zero is forbidden. For example, the output for the empty graph's treewidth is the sign bit 1 followed by the magnitude bit 1. Exact numerical equality is part of the algorithm's task; it is not an additional demand for an exact-value benchmark answer.

A deterministic multitape Turing machine has one finite program, a finite tape alphabet, a read-only binary input tape, finitely many work tapes initially blank, and a binary output tape. A transition inspects or changes only the scanned symbol on each tape and moves each head by at most one cell. Time counts all transitions, including reading the graph, arithmetic, preprocessing and writing the answer. There is no oracle, random tape, advice depending on input length, unbounded-word unit-cost arithmetic or free preprocessing. The polynomial clock is worst case and applies to every bitstring, including malformed encodings and encodings of nonplanar graphs. On those inputs, correctness and the output format are unrestricted. Imposing this total clock does not change the promised polynomial-time question, because a candidate machine with fixed bounds can be stopped at its own polynomial clock.

An algorithm returning only the exact minimum width suffices; an optimal tree decomposition need not be printed. Conversely, any polynomial-time algorithm producing an optimal decomposition would also answer this question. Fixed-parameter algorithms whose dependence on treewidth is superpolynomial do not give the required single polynomial bound when treewidth is unrestricted.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the exact algorithm-existence proposition, or its full logical negation, using the definitions and encoding above.

A positive answer must specify a finite deterministic machine and fixed polynomial bound, prove the total clock, and prove that its output is the exact treewidth for every encoded planar graph. It must cover all sizes, components and treewidth values, without an embedding or decomposition in the input.

A negative answer must prove that for every finite deterministic machine \(M\) and every pair of integers \(C,k\ge1\), at least one of the following holds:
\[
\exists x\in\{0,1\}^{*}:\quad
M(x)\text{ does not halt within }C(|x|+1)^k\text{ transitions},
\]
or
\[
\exists G\text{ finite, simple and planar}:\quad
M(\operatorname{enc}(G))\text{ fails to halt with output }
\operatorname{bin}_{\pm}(\operatorname{tw}(G)).
\]
Failure includes a malformed output, an incorrect integer or nontermination. The graph or failing input may depend on the machine and its proposed bound. Refuting one particular algorithm is insufficient.

An NP-hardness proof together with a proof of \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) would give a negative answer; NP-hardness alone is not the negation of polynomial-time solvability. Here \(\mathrm P\) is uniform deterministic polynomial-time decision, and \(\mathrm{NP}\) is uniform nondeterministic polynomial-time decision, with acceptance on at least one branch and polynomial clocks on all branches. A result for branchwidth, a proper subclass of planar graphs, an approximation guarantee, or a polynomial-time procedure per output object with potentially superpolynomially many output objects does not establish the positive assertion by itself. This is a yes/no running-time question. The numerical \(1/100\) benchmark tolerance does not change the exact integer function computed by its hypothetical algorithm.
